title: With virtual nodes, a failed server's load scatters over many neighbours
caption: Server A owns many small arcs (A#1, A#2, A#3 …). When it dies, each arc falls to whichever server comes next after it.

steps.text: Each physical server is hashed onto the ring many times (A#1, A#2, … often 100–200 points), so it owns many small arcs spread around the circle.
When A fails, each arc passes to the next point clockwise, and those points belong to different servers.
B, C and D each absorb about a third of A's keys. With one point per server, a single neighbour would take all of it and could fail next.

scenarios.name: Alternative: one point each
scenarios.summary: Without virtual nodes a failed server's whole arc goes to its single successor, which doubles its load and can cascade. Vnodes cost a bigger lookup table; that's all.
scenarios.caption: One point per server: A's single arc passes in one piece to the next server clockwise.

steps.text: A owns one contiguous arc, about a quarter of the ring.
A fails and the whole arc falls to B, the next point clockwise.
B's load doubles while C and D carry on as before. If B tips over, its double arc moves to the next server: a cascade.

scenarios.name: A comes back
scenarios.summary: When A rejoins, its arcs return from B, C and D at once. Keys written while it was away make A's old copies stale, so flush A's cache on rejoin.

steps.text: A restarts with its old cache contents and rejoins at the same points.
Its arcs move back from B, C and D: each loses a few small slices, so the shift is gradual and spread out.
Values updated while A was away now come from A's old copies: stale reads. Start A empty (or bump a cache epoch) and let it warm up.
